shanti.1: Om. O gods, may we hear with our ears what is good; O you who are worthy of worship, may we see with our eyes what is good. With steady limbs and bodies, praising you, may we live out the span of life the gods have set. May Indra of great fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, who knows all, grant us well-being. May Tārkṣya, whose wheel no one can harm, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati grant us well-being. Om, peace, peace, peace.

The śānti pāṭha of the Upaniṣads of the Atharvaveda (Praśna, Muṇḍaka, Māṇḍūkya), from the Ṛgveda (1.89.8 and 1.89.6). Tārkṣya is Garuḍa; ariṣṭanemi, “whose wheel-rim is unharmed”, is also read “who wards off harm”. Peace is said three times, for freedom from the troubles that come from oneself, from other beings and from the powers of nature.
1.1: Om. Sukeśā Bhāradvāja, Śaibya Satyakāma, Sauryāyaṇī Gārgya, Kausalya Āśvalāyana, Bhārgava Vaidarbhi and Kabandhī Kātyāyana — these, devoted to Brahman, steadfast in Brahman, seeking the supreme Brahman, in the belief that he would tell them all of it, came with fuel-sticks in hand to the revered Pippalāda. ॥1.1॥
Śaṅkara reads “devoted to Brahman” and “steadfast in Brahman” of the lower Brahman: they held it as the highest and were steadfast in its practice, and now sought the supreme Brahman.
1.2: The seer said to them: Once more, with austerity, continence and faith, live here for a year; then ask whatever questions you wish. If we know, we shall tell you everything. ॥1.2॥
1.3: Then Kabandhī Kātyāyana came to him and asked: Revered sir, from where are these creatures born? ॥1.3॥
1.4: Pippalāda said to him: Prajāpati, the lord of creatures, desiring creatures, performed austerity. Having performed austerity, he brought forth a pair, rayi, the food, and prāṇa, its eater, thinking: These two will make creatures for me in many ways. ॥1.4॥
1.5: The sun is prāṇa, and the moon is rayi. All this is rayi, both the formed and the formless; therefore form itself is rayi. ॥1.5॥
1.6: Now when the sun, rising, enters the eastern quarter, it thereby holds the living beings of the east in its rays. When it enters the south, the west, the north, the regions below and above and the quarters between, when it lights up everything, it thereby holds all living beings in its rays. ॥1.6॥
1.7: He it is who rises: Vaiśvānara, the self of all, of every form, prāṇa and fire. A ṛc, a verse of the Veda, declares this too: ॥1.7॥
1.8: The knowers of Brahman knew him as having all forms, full of rays, knowing all, the final refuge, the one light, the giver of heat. Thousand-rayed, existing in a hundred ways, the prāṇa of creatures, this sun rises. ॥1.8॥
The first two lines have no verb; Śaṅkara supplies it: the knowers of Brahman knew the sun so.
1.9: The year is Prajāpati; its two courses are the southern and the northern. So those who worship sacrifice and works of public good as what is done win only the world of the moon; it is they who come back again. Therefore these seers, desiring offspring, take the southern course. The path of the fathers is rayi. ॥1.9॥
Śaṅkara: they worship only what is done, the work that is made, not the eternal that is not made; so they win the world of the moon and come back when the merit of their work is spent.
1.10: But by the northern course, through austerity, continence, faith and knowledge, seeking the Self, they win the sun. This is the abode of the prāṇas; this is the immortal, the fearless; this is the final goal; from here they do not return. This is the barrier. On this there is a verse: ॥1.10॥
Śaṅkara: this is a barrier for those who do not know; they are held back from the sun.
1.11: Some call him the father, five-footed, of twelve forms, full of water, dwelling in the higher half beyond the sky. Others again call him the all-seeing, and say that all this is set in him, seven-wheeled and six-spoked. ॥1.11॥

Śaṅkara: the father is the sun as the year; his five feet are the seasons (the cold and the cool season counted as one), his twelve forms the months; the seven wheels are his seven horses, the six spokes the six seasons.
1.12: The month is Prajāpati; its dark half is rayi, and the bright half prāṇa. Therefore these seers perform sacrifice in the bright half, and the others in the other. ॥1.12॥
Śaṅkara: these seers see prāṇa in everything, so even when they sacrifice in the dark half they do it in the bright half; the others, even when they sacrifice in the bright half, do it in the dark.
1.13: Day and night are Prajāpati; the day is its prāṇa, and the night its rayi. Those who join in sexual union by day spill away their prāṇa. That they join in union by night is continence itself. ॥1.13॥
1.14: Food is Prajāpati; from it comes seed. From that these creatures are born. ॥1.14॥
1.15: So those who keep the vow of Prajāpati bring forth a pair, a son and a daughter. Theirs alone is this world of Brahmā who have austerity and continence, and in whom truth is established. ॥1.15॥

Śaṅkara: this world of Brahmā is the world of the moon, reached by the path of the fathers; the stainless one of the next mantra is the sun's, reached by the northern course. The vow of Prajāpati is to go to one's wife only in her season.
1.16: Theirs is that stainless world of Brahmā, in whom there is no crookedness, no falsehood, and no deceit. ॥1.16॥
1.iti: Here ends the first question of the Praśna Upaniṣad.
2.1: Then Bhārgava Vaidarbhi asked him: Revered sir, how many deities uphold a created being? Which of them make this manifest? And which of them is the greatest? ॥2.1॥
Śaṅkara: the created being here is the body, and to make this manifest is to proclaim their own greatness.
2.2: Pippalāda said to him: Space is such a deity, and wind, fire, water, earth, speech, mind, eye and ear. Making their greatness known, they declare: We prop up this body and uphold it. ॥2.2॥
2.3: Prāṇa, the greatest, said to them: Do not fall into delusion. It is I who, dividing myself fivefold, prop up this body and uphold it. They did not believe him. ॥2.3॥
2.4: Out of pride he rose upward, as if to leave. As he was leaving, all the others left too; and when he settled, all settled. As, when the king of the bees goes out, all the bees go out, and when he settles, all settle, so speech, mind, eye and ear, well pleased, praise prāṇa: ॥2.4॥
2.5: As fire he burns; he is the sun; he is the rain-cloud, he is Maghavan, Indra; he is the wind; he, the god, is the earth and rayi; he is being and non-being, and what is immortal. ॥2.5॥
Śaṅkara takes being and non-being as what has form and what is formless.
2.6: Like spokes in the hub of a chariot wheel, all is set in prāṇa: the ṛcs, the yajus and the sāmans of the Vedas, the sacrifice, the warrior and the priestly orders. ॥2.6॥
2.7: As Prajāpati you move in the womb; it is you who are born again. To you, O prāṇa, these creatures bring offerings, to you who dwell with the prāṇas, the senses. ॥2.7॥
2.8: For the gods you are the best bearer of offerings; for the fathers, the first svadhā offering; you are the true conduct of the seers, the Atharvāṅgirasas. ॥2.8॥
2.9: You, O prāṇa, are Indra; by your might you are Rudra, and the protector on every side. You move in the mid-air; you are the sun, the lord of the lights. ॥2.9॥
2.10: When you pour down rain, O prāṇa, these creatures of yours are filled with joy, thinking there will be food as much as they wish. ॥2.10॥
2.11: You, O prāṇa, are a vrātya, unconsecrated; you are the Ekarṣi fire, the eater, the true lord of all. We are the givers of what you eat; you, O Mātariśvan, are our father. ॥2.11॥
Vrātya, “unconsecrated”: Śaṅkara says prāṇa was born first, so there was no one to consecrate him; he is pure by nature. He also gives the reading “you are the father of Mātariśvan, the wind”.
2.12: The form of yours that abides in speech, in the ear and in the eye, and that spreads through the mind — make it benign; do not go out. ॥2.12॥
2.13: All this is in the power of prāṇa, and whatever is set in the third heaven. Guard us as a mother guards her children; grant us fortune and wisdom. ॥2.13॥
2.iti: Here ends the second question of the Praśna Upaniṣad.
3.1: Then Kausalya Āśvalāyana asked him: Revered sir, from where is this prāṇa born? How does it come into this body? Having divided itself, how does it abide? By what does it depart? How does it uphold the outer, and how the inner? ॥3.1॥
3.2: Pippalāda said to him: You ask questions that go beyond the bounds; you are a supreme knower of Brahman, and so I tell you. ॥3.2॥
3.3: This prāṇa is born from the Self. As a shadow goes with a person, so this prāṇa is spread out on the Self. By the doings of the mind it comes into this body. ॥3.3॥
3.4: As an emperor himself appoints his officers, telling them to rule over these villages and those, in the same way this prāṇa places the other prāṇas each in its own place, apart. ॥3.4॥
3.5: It places apāna in the organs of excretion and generation; prāṇa itself abides in the eye and the ear, passing through the mouth and the nose; and in the middle is samāna, for it carries evenly the food offered as an oblation. Therefore these seven flames arise. ॥3.5॥
Śaṅkara: the food eaten is an oblation into the fire within; from that fire, through the senses of the head, come the seven flames, seeing, hearing and the other perceptions.
3.6: This self is in the heart. Here there are a hundred and one channels. Each of them has a hundred branches, and each of these has seventy-two thousand smaller branch channels. In these moves vyāna. ॥3.6॥
3.7: And rising upward through one of them, udāna leads by merit to a world of merit, by sin to one of sin, and by both to the world of men. ॥3.7॥
3.8: The sun is the outer prāṇa; it rises, favouring this prāṇa that is in the eye. The deity that is in the earth holds a person's apāna; the space between is samāna; the wind is vyāna. ॥3.8॥
3.9: Tejas, fire, is udāna; so one whose fire has died down goes to rebirth with the senses merging into the mind. ॥3.9॥
3.10: Whatever is in his mind at death, with that he comes to prāṇa; and prāṇa, joined with fire (udāna), together with the self, leads him to the world he has willed. ॥3.10॥
3.11: The wise man who knows prāṇa thus — his offspring is never lost; he becomes immortal. On this there is a verse: ॥3.11॥
3.12: The origin of prāṇa, its coming, its seat, its fivefold sovereignty and its form within the body — knowing these, one attains immortality; knowing these, one attains immortality. ॥3.12॥
3.iti: Here ends the third question of the Praśna Upaniṣad.
4.1: Then Sauryāyaṇī Gārgya asked him: Revered sir, in this person which are they that sleep, and which stay awake in him? Which god is it that sees dreams? Whose is this happiness? In what, then, do all of them come to rest? ॥4.1॥
4.2: Pippalāda said to him: Gārgya, as the rays of the setting sun, all of them, become one in this disc of light, and spread out once more each time it rises again; just so, indeed, all that becomes one in the higher god, the mind. Therefore this person then does not hear, does not see, does not smell, does not taste, does not touch, does not speak, does not take, does not enjoy pleasure, does not excrete, does not move about; people say: he sleeps. ॥4.2॥
Śaṅkara: the mind is the higher god because the eye and the other gods of the body depend on it; all that is the senses with their objects.
4.3: In this city, the body, the fires of prāṇa alone stay awake. Apāna is the gārhapatya, the householder's fire; vyāna is the anvāhāryapacana, the southern fire; and because the fire is led forth from the gārhapatya, from this leading forth prāṇa is the āhavanīya, the fire of offering. ॥4.3॥

Śaṅkara: as the āhavanīya is carried from the gārhapatya at the fire offering, so prāṇa, moving through the mouth and nose, is led forth as it were from apāna; vyāna is the southern fire because it goes out from the heart by its southern opening.
4.4: Because it carries evenly these two offerings, the in-breath and the out-breath, it is samāna. The mind is indeed the sacrificer, and udāna is the very fruit of the sacrifice. Udāna leads this sacrificer day after day to Brahman. ॥4.4॥

Śaṅkara: samāna, which carries the two offerings, is the priest; in deep sleep udāna draws the mind away even from dreaming and brings it every day to Brahman, the Imperishable, as the sacrifice brings the sacrificer to heaven.
4.5: Here, in dream, this god experiences greatness. Whatever was seen, he sees once more; whatever was heard, that very thing he hears once more; what he has experienced in other lands and other quarters he experiences again and again; the seen and the unseen, the heard and the unheard, the experienced and the unexperienced, the real and the unreal: he sees it all; being all, he sees. ॥4.5॥

Śaṅkara: this god is the mind; the unseen and the unheard are what was seen and heard in another birth, for there is no impression of what was never experienced; the real is real water, the unreal the water of a mirage.
4.6: When he is overpowered by tejas, fire, then this god sees no dreams; and then, in this body, this happiness comes about. ॥4.6॥

Śaṅkara: he is the god who is the mind; tejas is the sun's heat called bile, lying in the channels, which shuts the doors of the impressions; the mind then pervades the whole body without distinctions, and that is deep sleep.
4.7: My dear, as birds go to rest in the tree where they roost, so indeed all that comes to rest in the supreme Self: ॥4.7॥
4.8: earth and the subtle measure of earth, water and the subtle measure of water, fire and the subtle measure of fire, air and the subtle measure of air, space and the subtle measure of space; the eye and what is to be seen, the ear and what is to be heard, the nose and what is to be smelt, the sense of taste and what is to be tasted, the skin and what is to be touched, speech and what is to be spoken, the hands and what is to be taken, the organ of generation and its delight, the organ of excretion and what is to be let go, the feet and where one is to go, the mind and what is to be thought, the intellect and what is to be understood, the ego and what is to be claimed as I, citta, awareness, and what is to be known by it, light and what is to be lit up, and prāṇa and what is to be held together by it. ॥4.8॥
Śaṅkara: the measures are the subtle elements; light here is the luminous skin, distinct from the organ of touch, and prāṇa is the thread on which all is strung.
4.9: For it is he who sees, touches, hears, smells, tastes, thinks, understands and acts, the self whose nature is knowing, the person. He comes to rest in the supreme, imperishable Self. ॥4.9॥
4.10: He attains the supreme Imperishable itself who knows that which is without shadow, without body, without redness, the pure, the Imperishable. He who knows it, my dear, becomes all-knowing and becomes all. On this there is a verse: ॥4.10॥
Śaṅkara: without shadow is without darkness; without body, free of every adjunct of name and form; without redness, free of red and every other quality.
4.11: That in which the self whose nature is knowing, with all the gods, and the prāṇas, that is the senses, and the elements come to rest — he who knows that Imperishable, my dear, becomes all-knowing and enters into all. ॥4.11॥
Śaṅkara: the gods are Agni and the other deities, the prāṇas the eye and the other senses, the elements earth and the rest.
4.iti: Here ends the fourth question of the Praśna Upaniṣad.
5.1: Then Śaibya Satyakāma asked him: Revered sir, the one among men who meditates on Om right up to his death, a wondrous thing — which world, truly, does he win by that? Pippalāda said to him: ॥5.1॥
Śaṅkara reads tat, that, as that wondrous thing: meditation on Om for the whole of life, until death.
5.2: Satyakāma, this which is Om is indeed the higher and the lower Brahman. So the one who knows this reaches, by this support alone, the one or the other. ॥5.2॥
Śaṅkara: the higher Brahman is the true, imperishable Person; the lower is prāṇa, the first-born. Om is the symbol of both.
5.3: If he meditates on Om of one measure, then, enlightened by that alone, he swiftly comes to the earth. The ṛcs bring him to the world of men, and there, endowed with austerity, continence and faith, he experiences greatness. ॥5.3॥
5.4: But if, through Om of two measures, he becomes one with the mind, he is led up by the yajus to the mid-air, to the world of Soma, the moon. Having enjoyed its splendour in the world of Soma, he returns again. ॥5.4॥

Śaṅkara: the second measure is the Yajurveda; one who meditates on it becomes one with the mind, whose deity is Soma, the moon; the yajus bring him to birth in the world of the moon, from where he returns to the world of men.
5.5: But he who meditates on this, the syllable Om of three measures, as the supreme Person becomes one with the light, the sun. As a snake is freed from its skin, so indeed is he freed from sin, and the sāmans lead him up to the world of Brahmā. There he beholds the Person who dwells in the city of the body, higher than this jīvaghana, the high mass of all lives. On this there are these two verses: ॥5.5॥

Śaṅkara takes the instrumental, by the syllable of three measures, as the object, because the context is meditation on Om: one meditates on the three-measured Om as the supreme Person; the plain grammar gives meditating on the supreme Person by means of the syllable Om. The jīvaghana is Hiraṇyagarbha, in whom all lives are gathered, and the world of Brahmā is his world.
5.6: The three measures, when employed, are subject to death; joined to one another, and each applied to its own object, when the acts outer, inner and middle are rightly performed, the knower does not waver. ॥5.6॥
Śaṅkara: the three measures are a, u and m; the outer, inner and middle acts are the meditations on the Person of waking, of dream and of deep sleep, made together in one act of meditation.
5.7: By the ṛcs, this world; by the yajus, the mid-air; by the sāmans, that which the wise know: the knower reaches it by Om alone as his support, and that too which is peaceful, ageless, immortal, fearless and supreme. ॥5.7॥
5.iti: Here ends the fifth question of the Praśna Upaniṣad.
6.1: Then Sukeśā Bhāradvāja asked him: Revered sir, Hiraṇyanābha, a prince of Kosala, came to me and asked this question: Bhāradvāja, do you know the Person of sixteen parts? I told the young man: I do not know him. Had I known him, why would I not have told you? He who speaks untruth withers away, root and all; therefore I may not speak untruth. Without a word he climbed into his chariot and went away. It is about him that I ask you: where is that Person? ॥6.1॥
6.2: Pippalāda said to him: My dear, right here within the body is that Person in whom these sixteen parts arise. ॥6.2॥
Śaṅkara: within the body, in the space of the lotus of the heart; the Person is not bounded by the body, but he is found there through seeing, hearing and thinking, and so it is said.
6.3: He reflected: What is it on whose departure I shall have departed, or on whose remaining I shall remain? ॥6.3॥
6.4: He created prāṇa; from prāṇa, faith; space, air, light, water, earth, the senses and the mind; food, and from food vigour; austerity, the mantras, works, the worlds, and in the worlds, name. ॥6.4॥

Śaṅkara: this prāṇa is Hiraṇyagarbha, the inner self of all beings; faith moves beings to good works, the worlds are the fruits of works, and name is the names of the beings born in them. These are the sixteen parts.
6.5: As these flowing rivers, bound for the sea, on reaching the sea disappear, their names and forms are lost, and it is called simply the sea; just so these sixteen parts of this all-seeing witness, bound for the Person, on reaching the Person disappear; their names and forms are lost, and it is called simply the Person. Then he becomes partless and immortal. On this there is a verse: ॥6.5॥
Śaṅkara: he is the one who knows this, shown by the teacher how the parts dissolve; death comes from the parts made by ignorance, so being without parts he is immortal.
6.6: The Person in whom the parts are set like spokes in the hub of a chariot wheel — know him, the Person who is to be known, so that death may not afflict you. ॥6.6॥
6.7: Pippalāda said to them: I know this supreme Brahman as just this much; there is nothing higher than this. ॥6.7॥
Śaṅkara: the supreme Brahman to be known is just this much; Pippalāda said so that the seekers would not suspect anything remained to be known, and would know their purpose fulfilled.
6.8: Worshipping him, they said: You indeed are our father, who take us across to the far shore of our ignorance. Salutation to the supreme seers; salutation to the supreme seers. ॥6.8॥

Śaṅkara: the teacher is their father because by knowledge he brings to birth the body of Brahman, free of age and death; the supreme seers are those who handed down the knowledge of Brahman, and the salutation is repeated for reverence.
Said twice, the salutation also marks the end of the Upaniṣad.
6.iti: Here ends the sixth question of the Praśna Upaniṣad.

shanti.1: Om. O gods, may we hear with our ears what is good; O you who are worthy of worship, may we see with our eyes what is good.
With steady limbs and bodies, praising you, may we live out the span of life the gods have set.
May Indra of great fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, who knows all, grant us well-being.
May Tārkṣya, whose wheel no one can harm, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati grant us well-being.
1.1: Om. Sukeśā Bhāradvāja, Śaibya Satyakāma, Sauryāyaṇī Gārgya,
Kausalya Āśvalāyana, Bhārgava Vaidarbhi and Kabandhī Kātyāyana — these,

in the belief that he would tell them all of it, came with fuel-sticks in hand to the revered Pippalāda. ॥1.1॥

live here for a year; then ask whatever questions you wish.
If we know, we shall tell you everything. ॥1.2॥
1.3: Then Kabandhī Kātyāyana came to him and asked:
Revered sir, from where are these creatures born? ॥1.3॥
1.4: Pippalāda said to him: Prajāpati, the lord of creatures, desiring creatures, performed austerity.
Having performed austerity, he brought forth a pair, rayi, the food, and prāṇa, its eater,
thinking: These two will make creatures for me in many ways. ॥1.4॥
1.5: The sun is prāṇa, and the moon is rayi. All this is rayi,
both the formed and the formless; therefore form itself is rayi. ॥1.5॥
1.6: Now when the sun, rising, enters the eastern quarter,
it thereby holds the living beings of the east in its rays.
When it enters the south, the west, the north, the regions below and above and the quarters between, when it lights up everything,
it thereby holds all living beings in its rays. ॥1.6॥
1.7: He it is who rises: Vaiśvānara, the self of all, of every form, prāṇa and fire.
A ṛc, a verse of the Veda, declares this too: ॥1.7॥
1.8: The knowers of Brahman knew him as having all forms, full of rays, knowing all,
the final refuge, the one light, the giver of heat.
Thousand-rayed, existing in a hundred ways,
the prāṇa of creatures, this sun rises. ॥1.8॥
1.9: The year is Prajāpati; its two courses are the southern and the northern.
So those who worship sacrifice and works of public good as what is done
win only the world of the moon; it is they who come back again.
Therefore these seers, desiring offspring, take the southern course.
The path of the fathers is rayi. ॥1.9॥
1.10: But by the northern course, through austerity, continence, faith
and knowledge, seeking the Self, they win the sun.
This is the abode of the prāṇas; this is the immortal, the fearless; this is the final goal; from here they do not return.
This is the barrier. On this there is a verse: ॥1.10॥
1.11: Some call him the father, five-footed, of twelve forms,
full of water, dwelling in the higher half beyond the sky.
Others again call him the all-seeing,
and say that all this is set in him, seven-wheeled and six-spoked. ॥1.11॥
1.12: The month is Prajāpati; its dark half is rayi, and the bright half prāṇa.
Therefore these seers perform sacrifice in the bright half, and the others in the other. ॥1.12॥
1.13: Day and night are Prajāpati; the day is its prāṇa, and the night its rayi.
Those who join in sexual union by day spill away their prāṇa.
That they join in union by night is continence itself. ॥1.13॥
1.14: Food is Prajāpati; from it comes seed.
From that these creatures are born. ॥1.14॥
1.15: So those who keep the vow of Prajāpati bring forth a pair, a son and a daughter.
Theirs alone is this world of Brahmā who have austerity and continence,
and in whom truth is established. ॥1.15॥
1.16: Theirs is that stainless world of Brahmā, in whom there is no crookedness, no falsehood,
1.iti: Here ends the first question of the Praśna Upaniṣad.
2.1: Revered sir, how many deities uphold a created being? Which of them make this manifest?
And which of them is the greatest? ॥2.1॥
2.2: Pippalāda said to him: Space is such a deity, and wind, fire, water,
earth, speech, mind, eye and ear. Making their greatness known, they declare:
We prop up this body and uphold it. ॥2.2॥
2.3: Prāṇa, the greatest, said to them: Do not fall into delusion.
It is I who, dividing myself fivefold, prop up this body and uphold it.
2.4: Out of pride he rose upward, as if to leave.
As he was leaving, all the others left too; and when he settled, all settled.
As, when the king of the bees goes out, all the bees go out,
and when he settles, all settle,
so speech, mind, eye and ear, well pleased, praise prāṇa: ॥2.4॥
2.5: As fire he burns; he is the sun;
he is the rain-cloud, he is Maghavan, Indra; he is the wind;
he, the god, is the earth and rayi;
he is being and non-being, and what is immortal. ॥2.5॥
2.6: Like spokes in the hub of a chariot wheel, all is set in prāṇa:
the ṛcs, the yajus and the sāmans of the Vedas, the sacrifice, the warrior and the priestly orders. ॥2.6॥
2.7: As Prajāpati you move in the womb; it is you who are born again.
To you, O prāṇa, these creatures bring offerings,
to you who dwell with the prāṇas, the senses. ॥2.7॥
2.8: For the gods you are the best bearer of offerings; for the fathers, the first svadhā offering;
you are the true conduct of the seers, the Atharvāṅgirasas. ॥2.8॥
2.9: You, O prāṇa, are Indra; by your might you are Rudra, and the protector on every side.
You move in the mid-air; you are the sun, the lord of the lights. ॥2.9॥
2.10: When you pour down rain, O prāṇa,
these creatures of yours are filled with joy, thinking there will be food as much as they wish. ॥2.10॥
2.11: You, O prāṇa, are a vrātya, unconsecrated; you are the Ekarṣi fire, the eater, the true lord of all.
We are the givers of what you eat; you, O Mātariśvan, are our father. ॥2.11॥
2.12: The form of yours that abides in speech, in the ear and in the eye,
and that spreads through the mind — make it benign; do not go out. ॥2.12॥
2.13: All this is in the power of prāṇa, and whatever is set in the third heaven.
Guard us as a mother guards her children; grant us fortune and wisdom. ॥2.13॥
2.iti: Here ends the second question of the Praśna Upaniṣad.
3.1: Revered sir, from where is this prāṇa born? How does it come into this body?
Having divided itself, how does it abide? By what does it depart? How does it uphold the outer,
3.2: Pippalāda said to him: You ask questions that go beyond the bounds; you are a supreme knower of Brahman,
3.3: This prāṇa is born from the Self.
As a shadow goes with a person, so this prāṇa is spread out on the Self.
By the doings of the mind it comes into this body. ॥3.3॥
3.4: As an emperor himself appoints his officers,
telling them to rule over these villages and those, in the same way this prāṇa places the other prāṇas
each in its own place, apart. ॥3.4॥
3.5: It places apāna in the organs of excretion and generation; prāṇa itself abides in the eye and the ear, passing through the mouth and the nose;
and in the middle is samāna, for it carries evenly the food offered as an oblation.
3.6: This self is in the heart. Here there are a hundred and one channels.
Each of them has a hundred branches, and each of these has seventy-two thousand smaller branch channels.
3.7: And rising upward through one of them, udāna leads by merit to a world of merit,
by sin to one of sin, and by both to the world of men. ॥3.7॥
3.8: The sun is the outer prāṇa; it rises,
favouring this prāṇa that is in the eye.
The deity that is in the earth holds a person's apāna; the space between is samāna; the wind is vyāna. ॥3.8॥
3.9: Tejas, fire, is udāna; so one whose fire has died down goes to rebirth
with the senses merging into the mind. ॥3.9॥
3.10: Whatever is in his mind at death, with that he comes to prāṇa; and prāṇa, joined with fire (udāna), together with the self,
leads him to the world he has willed. ॥3.10॥
3.11: The wise man who knows prāṇa thus — his offspring is never lost;
he becomes immortal. On this there is a verse: ॥3.11॥
3.12: The origin of prāṇa, its coming, its seat, its fivefold sovereignty
and its form within the body — knowing these, one attains immortality;
3.iti: Here ends the third question of the Praśna Upaniṣad.
4.1: Then Sauryāyaṇī Gārgya asked him: Revered sir, in this person
which are they that sleep, and which stay awake in him? Which god is it that sees dreams?
Whose is this happiness? In what, then, do all of them come to rest? ॥4.1॥
4.2: Pippalāda said to him: Gārgya, as the rays of the setting sun, all of them,
become one in this disc of light, and spread out once more each time it rises again;
just so, indeed, all that becomes one in the higher god, the mind.
Therefore this person then does not hear, does not see, does not smell, does not taste, does not touch, does not speak,
does not take, does not enjoy pleasure, does not excrete, does not move about; people say: he sleeps. ॥4.2॥
4.3: In this city, the body, the fires of prāṇa alone stay awake. Apāna is the gārhapatya, the householder's fire;
vyāna is the anvāhāryapacana, the southern fire; and because the fire is led forth from the gārhapatya, from this leading forth
prāṇa is the āhavanīya, the fire of offering. ॥4.3॥
4.4: Because it carries evenly these two offerings, the in-breath and the out-breath, it is samāna.
The mind is indeed the sacrificer, and udāna is the very fruit of the sacrifice.
Udāna leads this sacrificer day after day to Brahman. ॥4.4॥
4.5: Here, in dream, this god experiences greatness.
Whatever was seen, he sees once more; whatever was heard, that very thing he hears once more;
what he has experienced in other lands and other quarters he experiences again and again;
the seen and the unseen, the heard and the unheard, the experienced and the unexperienced,
the real and the unreal: he sees it all; being all, he sees. ॥4.5॥
4.6: When he is overpowered by tejas, fire,
then this god sees no dreams; and then, in this body, this happiness comes about. ॥4.6॥
4.7: My dear, as birds go to rest in the tree where they roost,
so indeed all that comes to rest in the supreme Self: ॥4.7॥
4.8: earth and the subtle measure of earth, water and the subtle measure of water, fire and the subtle measure of fire,
air and the subtle measure of air, space and the subtle measure of space; the eye and what is to be seen,
the ear and what is to be heard, the nose and what is to be smelt,
the sense of taste and what is to be tasted, the skin and what is to be touched, speech and what is to be spoken,
the hands and what is to be taken, the organ of generation and its delight, the organ of excretion and what is to be let go,
the feet and where one is to go, the mind and what is to be thought, the intellect and what is to be understood,
the ego and what is to be claimed as I, citta, awareness, and what is to be known by it,
light and what is to be lit up, and prāṇa and what is to be held together by it. ॥4.8॥
4.9: For it is he who sees, touches, hears, smells, tastes, thinks, understands and acts,
the self whose nature is knowing, the person. He comes to rest in the supreme, imperishable Self. ॥4.9॥
4.10: He attains the supreme Imperishable itself who knows that which is without shadow, without body, without redness,
the pure, the Imperishable. He who knows it, my dear, becomes all-knowing and becomes all.
On this there is a verse: ॥4.10॥
4.11: That in which the self whose nature is knowing, with all the gods, and the prāṇas, that is the senses, and the elements come to rest —
he who knows that Imperishable, my dear, becomes all-knowing and enters into all. ॥4.11॥
4.iti: Here ends the fourth question of the Praśna Upaniṣad.
5.1: Revered sir, the one among men who meditates on Om right up to his death, a wondrous thing —
which world, truly, does he win by that? Pippalāda said to him: ॥5.1॥
5.2: Satyakāma, this which is Om is indeed the higher and the lower Brahman.
So the one who knows this reaches, by this support alone, the one or the other. ॥5.2॥
5.3: If he meditates on Om of one measure, then, enlightened by that alone,
he swiftly comes to the earth. The ṛcs bring him to the world of men, and there,
endowed with austerity, continence and faith, he experiences greatness. ॥5.3॥
5.4: But if, through Om of two measures, he becomes one with the mind,
he is led up by the yajus to the mid-air, to the world of Soma, the moon. Having enjoyed its splendour in the world of Soma,
5.5: But he who meditates on this, the syllable Om of three measures, as the supreme Person
becomes one with the light, the sun. As a snake is freed from its skin,
so indeed is he freed from sin, and the sāmans lead him up to the world of Brahmā.
There he beholds the Person who dwells in the city of the body, higher than this jīvaghana, the high mass of all lives.
On this there are these two verses: ॥5.5॥
5.6: The three measures, when employed, are subject to death;
joined to one another, and each applied to its own object,
when the acts outer, inner and middle
are rightly performed, the knower does not waver. ॥5.6॥
5.7: By the ṛcs, this world; by the yajus, the mid-air;
by the sāmans, that which the wise know:
the knower reaches it by Om alone as his support,
and that too which is peaceful, ageless, immortal, fearless and supreme. ॥5.7॥
5.iti: Here ends the fifth question of the Praśna Upaniṣad.
6.1: Then Sukeśā Bhāradvāja asked him: Revered sir, Hiraṇyanābha,
a prince of Kosala, came to me and asked this question:
Bhāradvāja, do you know the Person of sixteen parts? I told the young man: I do not know him.
Had I known him, why would I not have told you?
He who speaks untruth withers away, root and all; therefore I may not speak untruth.
Without a word he climbed into his chariot and went away. It is about him that I ask you:
6.2: Pippalāda said to him: My dear, right here within the body is that Person
in whom these sixteen parts arise. ॥6.2॥
6.3: He reflected: What is it on whose departure I shall have departed,
or on whose remaining I shall remain? ॥6.3॥
6.4: He created prāṇa; from prāṇa, faith; space, air, light, water, earth, the senses
and the mind; food, and from food vigour; austerity, the mantras, works, the worlds, and in the worlds, name. ॥6.4॥
6.5: As these flowing rivers, bound for the sea, on reaching the sea
disappear, their names and forms are lost, and it is called simply the sea;
just so these sixteen parts of this all-seeing witness, bound for the Person, on reaching the Person disappear;
their names and forms are lost, and it is called simply the Person. Then he becomes partless and immortal.
On this there is a verse: ॥6.5॥
6.6: The Person in whom the parts are set like spokes in the hub of a chariot wheel —
know him, the Person who is to be known, so that death may not afflict you. ॥6.6॥
6.7: Pippalāda said to them: I know this supreme Brahman as just this much;
there is nothing higher than this. ॥6.7॥
6.8: Worshipping him, they said: You indeed are our father,
who take us across to the far shore of our ignorance. Salutation to the supreme seers; salutation to the supreme seers. ॥6.8॥
6.iti: Here ends the sixth question of the Praśna Upaniṣad.
